articles.title: CIA, Authenticity, Non-Repudiation and AAA: The Vocabulary of Security
articles.scope: Defines confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity and non-repudiation (CISSP 2024 calls these the '5 Pillars'; the 2027 outline lists the same five) and the authentication, authorization and accounting model, which SY0-801 1.1 groups under defense in depth. Contrasts integrity with authenticity and authentication with accounting, and maps each objective to the controls and primitives that deliver it. Afterwards the reader can classify any control or incident by the objective it serves.

articles.title: Risk, Threats, Vulnerabilities and Controls
articles.scope: Separates threat, threat actor, vector, vulnerability, exploit, likelihood, impact, and inherent versus residual risk, and shows how they combine. Covers control categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and types (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive) with .NET/Angular examples. The risk-management process and frameworks belong to security/grc; this page owns the vocabulary.

articles.title: Threat Actors, Motivations, Threat Vectors and Attack Surfaces
articles.scope: Covers SY0-801 2.2 to 2.4: actor types (nation-state, organized crime, hacktivist, insider, unskilled, competitor, accidental), their motivations and attributes, and vectors (message, image and QR, file, browser, network, remote access, supply chain, removable media, human, IoT/OT, physical, signal). It also covers attack surfaces: unsupported or unmanaged systems, shadow IT, rogue devices, identity providers, public repositories and object storage, LLMs and stale credentials. It contrasts actor, vector and surface, treats insider threat as the concept behind insider-risk tooling, and links detection-response for malware and IoCs and ai-security for AI threats.

articles.title: Secure Design Principles: Least Privilege to Secure by Design
articles.scope: Teaches the Saltzer-Schroeder principles in their modern forms: least privilege versus need-to-know, separation of duties versus two-person integrity versus rotation of duties, secure defaults, and fail secure versus fail safe versus fail open (the SY0-801 failure modes). It also covers complete mediation, keep it simple and small, open design (Kerckhoffs), attack-surface reduction, and privacy by design with privacy-enhancing technologies, all from CISSP 2027 3.1. The 2024 outline's 'zero trust or trust but verify', shared responsibility, SASE, well-architected frameworks and the CISA Secure by Design pledge are linked as neighbours, and each principle gets a C# and a Python illustration.

articles.title: Defense in Depth vs Zero Trust vs Perimeter Security
articles.scope: Compares castle-and-moat perimeter security, layered defense in depth and zero trust, and explains why they complement each other; SY0-801 even lists zero trust principles under defense in depth. Shows how each fails (lateral movement, single-layer bypass, policy-engine outage), contrasts zero trust with 'trust but verify', and explains how identity became the primary perimeter.

articles.title: Zero Trust Architecture: NIST SP 800-207, PDP/PEP and Maturity Models
articles.scope: Works through NIST SP 800-207: tenets, policy engine, policy administrator and policy enforcement point, control and data planes, the three deployment approaches, and SP 800-207A for cloud-native apps. It maps the SY0-701 1.2 component list and the SY0-801 3.2 ZTA items (user authentication, device health and inventory, application access control). It then contrasts adoption models: CISA ZTMM 2.0 (five pillars, three cross-cutting capabilities, four stages), the Microsoft Zero Trust adoption framework, and NCCoE SP 1800-35 (final June 2025, 19 example implementations), and maps mTLS, workload identity, conditional access, continuous evaluation and micro-segmentation onto the tenets.

articles.title: Formal Security Models: Bell-LaPadula vs Biba vs Clark-Wilson vs Brewer-Nash
articles.scope: Contrasts Bell-LaPadula's simple security and star properties (plus the strong star property) with Biba's simple and star integrity axioms, which together make up the outline's 'Biba, Star, Bell-LaPadula'. Adds Clark-Wilson, Brewer-Nash, Graham-Denning, Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman, Take-Grant, lattice, information-flow and noninterference models, plus the reference monitor, security kernel and trusted computing base. It also shows where these ideas live on in SELinux mandatory access control, classification labels and tenant isolation.

articles.title: Security Implications of Architecture Models: On-Premises, Cloud, Serverless, Microservices, Virtualized, Containerized, IoT, OT/ICS, Embedded, Edge and Air-Gapped
articles.scope: Compares architecture models by attack surface, isolation boundary, patchability, responsibility split, resilience and recovery, covering the SY0-801 3.1 technical and business considerations. Works through the CISSP 3.5 vulnerability classes: database aggregation and inference, ICS, embedded, HPC, edge and distributed systems, supply chain risk, autonomous systems and quantum computing. Links security/cloud-security for shared responsibility and security/network-security for segmentation.

articles.title: Physical and Environmental Security: Site and Facility Design, CPTED, Perimeter and Internal Controls, Fire, Power and HVAC
articles.scope: Covers site selection and CPTED, layered physical controls from fence to rack (lighting, guards, badges, access control vestibules, locks, CCTV), and the rooms that need them: wiring closets, server rooms, and media and evidence storage. Also covers fire detection and suppression, power (UPS, generators), HVAC and environmental monitoring, physical attacks such as tailgating, badge cloning and skimming, physical penetration testing, and how cloud providers take over data-center controls under shared responsibility. Also covers (merged from data-center-and-physical-security): Logical, physical and environmental design, redundancy and resilience of provider data centers; how providers evidence physical controls; and what customers still own at the edge and on premises (Outposts, Azure Local).

articles.title: Systems Security Engineering and the Information System Lifecycle (NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1)
articles.scope: Teaches NIST SP 800-160 Vol. 1 Rev. 1 and the CISSP 3.10 lifecycle: stakeholder needs, requirements analysis, secure architectural design, implementation, integration, verification and validation, transition, operations and sustainment, continuous security review, and retirement with secure disposal. Shows how to select controls from system security requirements (3.3), and contrasts this system lifecycle with the software SDLC and with the RMF in security/grc.

articles.title: Product Assurance: Common Criteria vs FIPS 140-3 vs Service Attestations
articles.scope: Contrasts Common Criteria (ISO/IEC 15408: protection profiles, security targets, EAL1-7, CCRA recognition) with FIPS 140-3. FIPS 140-3 aligns with ISO/IEC 19790, is validated by the joint NIST and CCCS CMVP at levels 1-4, and replaced FIPS 140-2, whose validations became historical in September 2026; both product certifications are then contrasted with service attestations (SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, CSA STAR) published in provider trust portals, which belong to security/grc. Afterwards the reader can check whether a certificate's scope and validated configuration match their actual deployment.

articles.title: Enterprise Security Architecture Frameworks: SABSA, TOGAF Security Guidance and CSA Enterprise Architecture, with MCRA and AWS SRA as Inputs
articles.scope: Compares SABSA's business-attribute-driven layered matrix with TOGAF's security guidance and the CSA Enterprise Architecture. Treats the Microsoft Cybersecurity Reference Architectures and the AWS Security Reference Architecture as provider inputs, and shows how to trace business attributes to controls. The MCRA vs AWS SRA pair lives in cloud/compare and TOGAF itself in architecture/enterprise.

articles.title: Secure Baselines and Hardening: CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, SCAP and Configuration Drift
articles.scope: Walks through choosing a benchmark (CIS, STIG, or provider benchmarks such as MCSB and AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, linked) and tailoring it into a documented baseline with recorded exceptions. Covers applying the baseline as code (GPO, DSC, Ansible, IaC policy), assessing it with SCAP content (XCCDF, OVAL), and detecting drift for operating systems, containers and SaaS/PaaS settings. Cloud posture management (CSPM) is owned by security/cloud-security; move this page there if that section claims it.

articles.title: Security Capability Landscape: SIEM, SOAR, XDR, CSPM, CNAPP, DLP and Friends, and Where Each Is Taught
articles.scope: An orientation map with one-line contrasts of tool categories (SIEM vs SOAR vs XDR vs EDR, CSPM vs CWPP vs CNAPP, CASB vs SSE, DLP vs insider risk vs eDiscovery, WAF vs DDoS protection), mapped to the Microsoft and AWS product families. It only orients and links: the concepts belong to detection-response, cloud-security, network-security, data-protection and grc, and the products to cloud/azure and cloud/aws. It gives the SC-900 product domains a neutral entry point.

articles.title: Identification vs Authentication vs Authorization vs Accounting
articles.scope: Separates the AAA steps with request-level examples: identity proofing at enrollment, a claimed identity, proof of that claim, a permission decision and an audit record. Covers why 401 and 403 differ, claims versus permissions, and why OAuth is not an authentication protocol, with ASP.NET Core and FastAPI middleware side by side.

articles.title: Authentication Factors, MFA and NIST SP 800-63-4 Assurance Levels
articles.scope: Covers knowledge, possession and inherence factors: hard and soft tokens, OTP (HOTP/TOTP), push with number matching, backup codes, and biometrics with FAR, FRR and CER. Explains MFA bypass (fatigue, SIM swap, AiTM phishing, token theft), why phishing resistance is the real dividing line, and the IAL, AAL and FAL levels. An 'exam answer vs current guidance' box sets the SY0-801 password best-practice list (complexity, expiration, age) against NIST SP 800-63B-4: length over complexity, no forced expiry, breached-password checks.

articles.title: Passkeys, FIDO2 and WebAuthn: Synced vs Device-Bound Credentials
articles.scope: Explains how WebAuthn (Level 3, W3C Recommendation 2026-08-25) and CTAP form FIDO2. Credentials are scoped to a relying-party ID and every ceremony is checked against the calling origin, which is what makes them phishing-resistant. Contrasts platform authenticators such as Windows Hello for Business with roaming security keys, and synced with device-bound credentials (backup-eligible and backup-state flags; AAL2 vs AAL3). Also covers attestation, conditional mediation, related origins and the recovery path, with a registration and assertion server in C# and Python.

articles.title: Directory Services, LDAP, Kerberos and NTLM: On-Premises Identity Foundations
articles.scope: Explains directories, LDAP and LDAPS binds and searches, the Kerberos ticket model (KDC, TGT, service tickets), NTLM challenge-response and its deprecation, and service accounts including gMSAs. Contrasts ticket-based Kerberos with token-based OIDC to explain hybrid identity. Attacks are summarized here and compared in identity-attacks-compared; AD DS hardening is covered on cloud/azure/identity.

articles.title: Hybrid Identity Models: Directory Synchronization vs Pass-Through vs Federated Authentication
articles.scope: Compares the neutral models: synchronized identities with password-hash sync (cloud authentication), agent-based pass-through validation against on-premises directories, federation to an on-premises IdP, and cloud-only identity. Trade-offs covered are resilience when on-premises fails, leaked-credential detection, where MFA happens, and migration off federation. Entra Connect Sync, Cloud Sync and AD FS migration belong to cloud/azure/identity, and AWS Managed Microsoft AD vs AD Connector to cloud/aws/identity.

articles.title: Single Sign-On and Federation: SAML 2.0 vs OpenID Connect vs WS-Federation
articles.scope: Separates SSO within one trust domain from federation across domains, and defines identity provider, SAML service provider (not a cloud service provider) and relying party. Compares SAML assertions with OIDC ID tokens, XML signatures with JWS, and SP-initiated with IdP-initiated flows, treats WS-Federation as legacy, and covers B2B and B2C. Treats identity providers as an attack surface (SY0-801 2.4) and helps the reader pick a protocol for a SaaS integration, a SPA or a mobile app.

articles.title: Identity Architecture Patterns: Identity Broker, Hub-and-Spoke Federation, Home-Realm Discovery, Multi-Tenant SaaS and Cross-Organization Access
articles.scope: Gives identity design patterns for workforce, B2B, B2C and multicloud: an identity broker vs direct federation, hub-and-spoke trust, home-realm discovery, tenant isolation in multi-tenant SaaS, and cross-organization access and synchronization. Each pattern is weighed on blast radius, latency, resilience and lock-in, with provider specifics linked.

articles.title: OAuth 2.0 and OAuth 2.1: Roles, Scopes, Tokens and What Changed
articles.scope: Teaches the OAuth roles (resource owner, client, authorization server, resource server), scopes and consent, access and refresh tokens, and client types. Covers metadata and discovery (RFC 8414, RFC 9728, RFC 8707) and introspection and revocation (RFC 7662, RFC 7009). Explains what the still-draft OAuth 2.1 consolidates (PKCE everywhere, no implicit or password grants, exact redirect-URI matching) and that MCP authorization builds on it.

articles.title: OAuth Consent, Delegated vs Application Permissions, App Roles and Consent Phishing
articles.scope: Contrasts delegated permissions, where the effective right is the intersection of the app's grant and the user's own rights, with app-only application permissions and with app roles. Covers user vs admin consent, consent policies and app governance. Treats illicit consent grants and over-scoped agent and tool consent as top real-world risks, with detection and cleanup steps.

articles.title: Choosing an OAuth Flow: Authorization Code + PKCE, Client Credentials, Device Code, On-Behalf-Of and Token Exchange
articles.scope: A decision guide for SPAs, native and desktop apps, daemons, CLIs, TVs and API chains. Covers code + PKCE; native-app redirects per RFC 8252 (claimed HTTPS, loopback, private-use schemes), noting that BCP 212 now holds RFC 8252 and RFC 10017; client credentials (secret vs private_key_jwt vs mTLS vs federated assertion); the device grant (RFC 8628); refresh rotation; and CIBA. Contrasts RFC 8693 token exchange with the Microsoft identity platform's JWT-bearer-based on-behalf-of flow, explains why implicit and ROPC are deprecated, and shows each flow with MSAL in .NET and MSAL or Authlib in Python.

articles.title: OpenID Connect: ID Tokens, Claims, Discovery and Logout
articles.scope: Explains how OIDC adds authentication to OAuth: ID vs access tokens, standard claims, nonce and at_hash, discovery and JWKS rotation, UserInfo, the hybrid flow, and front-channel vs back-channel logout. Walks through the token validation a .NET or Python relying party must do and the classic mistakes, such as calling APIs with ID tokens or skipping audience checks.

articles.title: JWT, JWS and JWE: Token Formats, Validation and Pitfalls
articles.scope: Explains the JOSE family (JWS, JWE, JWK, JWA), JWT claims and the RFC 9068 access-token profile, and contrasts self-contained JWTs with opaque tokens checked by introspection. Uses RFC 8725 to catalogue the attacks: alg=none, RS/HS key confusion, kid and jku injection, missing audience checks and over-long lifetimes. Introduces SD-JWT (RFC 9901), with SD-JWT VC still a draft, and ends with a validation checklist in C# and Python.

articles.title: Hardening OAuth: RFC 9700, Browser-Based Apps (BCP 212), BFF and Sender-Constrained Tokens
articles.scope: Applies the RFC 9700 threats and mitigations: code injection, mix-up, open redirectors, token leakage, refresh replay and issuer identification (RFC 9207). Compares the RFC 10017 browser architectures (BFF, token-mediating backend, browser-only), PAR, JAR and RAR, and the two sender-constraining options, DPoP (RFC 9449) and mTLS-bound tokens (RFC 8705). Covers FAPI 2.0 (final February 2025: PAR, PKCE, sender-constrained tokens, private_key_jwt or mTLS client authentication), ending with an Angular plus ASP.NET Core BFF reference design.

articles.title: API and Service-to-Service Authorization Patterns: Edge vs In-Service Enforcement, Token Exchange, Phantom Tokens and Transaction Tokens
articles.scope: Contrasts coarse checks at the gateway with fine-grained checks inside the service. Compares forwarding vs exchanging tokens per hop (RFC 8693), with audience scoping. Covers the phantom-token pattern (opaque outside, JWT inside) and transaction tokens for internal call chains, then combines BFF, authorization engines and capability tokens into one design for microservices and agents.

articles.title: Session Management, Token Lifetimes, Revocation and Continuous Access Evaluation
articles.scope: Contrasts server-side cookie sessions with token-based sessions and covers lifetime trade-offs, refresh rotation, revocation, logout propagation, step-up with authentication context and acr values, and session-hijacking defenses. Explains event-driven revocation through the OpenID Shared Signals Framework, CAEP and RISC (all 1.0 final), and links Entra continuous access evaluation as the provider implementation.

articles.title: Device Identity and Device Trust: Registration, Device Certificates, TPM Attestation and Posture Signals
articles.scope: Treats devices as identities: registration vs join, device certificates and TPM-bound keys, attestation, and MDM compliance and posture (health, inventory). Shows how these signals feed zero trust decisions, and links security/network-security for NAC and 802.1X posture checks.

articles.title: Account Recovery and Credential Bootstrapping: SSPR, Temporary Passes, Backup Codes and Help-Desk Verification
articles.scope: Steps to issue a first credential and recover lost ones without reopening phishable paths. Covers identity proofing (SP 800-63A-4), time-limited bootstrap passes such as Entra Temporary Access Pass, backup and recovery codes, SSPR design, and help-desk verification that resists social engineering. Everything is checked against the SP 800-63B-4 recovery requirements.

articles.title: Identity Attacks Compared: Brute Force vs Password Spraying vs Credential Stuffing, MFA Fatigue, AiTM, Token Theft, Consent and Device-Code Phishing, Pass-the-Hash, Kerberoasting, Golden Tickets and Golden SAML
articles.scope: For each attack, gives the precondition, the observable signal and the defense. Covers the SY0-801 2.5 credential attacks (spraying, brute force, user enumeration, replay, MFA bypass), the CISSP 3.7 items (pass the hash, Kerberos exploitation, adversary-in-the-middle), 2FA fatigue, and device-code and consent phishing. Closes with AD DS resilience; detections are linked to detection-response.

articles.title: Identity Lifecycle, SCIM 2.0 and Identity Governance
articles.scope: Covers joiner-mover-leaver; SY0-801 account types (user, privileged global and local, service, third-party, emergency); and role definition and transition (CISSP 5.5). Contrasts SCIM 2.0 (RFC 7643/7644) with SAML/OIDC just-in-time provisioning, and HR-driven with request-driven and attribute-driven provisioning. Also covers entitlements and access packages, access reviews, SoD conflicts, orphaned accounts, privilege creep and guest lifecycles, linking Entra ID Governance and IAM Identity Center.

articles.title: Access Control Models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, Rule-Based, ABAC, ReBAC, PBAC, Time-Based, JIT and RAdAC
articles.scope: Compares the models by who sets policy, what a decision depends on, how they scale and how they fail (role explosion, attribute sprawl, graph depth). Disambiguates RBAC from RuBAC and ABAC (SP 800-162; in CISSP 5.4 but absent from SY0-801 4.5) from PBAC. Adds the SY0-801 time-based and just-in-time models, CISSP 2027 risk-adaptable access control ('risk based' in 2024), and ACLs vs capability tables, implementing one rule as an ASP.NET Core policy and in Python.

articles.title: Fine-Grained Authorization Engines: Zanzibar/OpenFGA vs OPA/Rego vs Cedar, and AuthZEN
articles.scope: Explains the PEP, PDP, PIP and PAP architecture inherited from XACML, and the Zanzibar model: tuples, check and expand, consistency tokens and the new-enemy problem. Compares OpenFGA (CNCF Incubating), SpiceDB, OPA/Rego (CNCF Graduated) and Cedar (CNCF Sandbox; Amazon Verified Permissions) on expressiveness, analyzability, latency and data-sync burden. Shows how the OpenID AuthZEN Authorization API 1.0 (final) standardizes the PEP-to-PDP call, and links devops for OPA admission control.

articles.title: Capability-Based Authorization vs RBAC and ACLs
articles.scope: Expands the existing stub. Contrasts object capabilities, where holding an unforgeable, attenuable reference is the permission, with identity-plus-role lookups and ACLs, and explains ambient authority and confused-deputy resistance. Covers attenuation and delegation (macaroons, Biscuit, UCAN), per-session grants for MCP tool servers and agents, revocation models, and the migration cost of designing capabilities in versus bolting on RBAC.

articles.title: Privileged Access Management: PAM vs PIM, Just-in-Time Access and Break-Glass
articles.scope: Contrasts standing privilege with JIT and zero standing privilege, and separates PAM, PIM, PASM and PEDM, with approvals, justification and just-enough-administration. Covers local vs global privileged accounts with rotated local admin passwords (for example Windows LAPS), credential vaulting, privilege escalation through admin groups or sudo and how to audit it, break-glass accounts, PAWs, jump hosts and secure terminal access over SSH and RDP. Also covers tiered administration and CIEM, and shows how privileged access controls break the ransomware kill chain, linking Entra PIM and AWS temporary elevated access.

articles.title: Workload Identity vs Static Credentials: SPIFFE/SPIRE, Federation and WIMSE
articles.scope: Expands the existing stub. Compares platform-issued, short-lived workload credentials with API keys, connection strings and .env secrets. Covers SPIFFE IDs and X.509/JWT SVIDs, SPIRE attestation, and workload identity federation from GitHub Actions or Kubernetes service accounts. Also covers the IETF WIMSE drafts, the self-hosted Docker Compose fallback, and leaked-credential blast radius, linking managed identities and IAM roles.

articles.title: mTLS vs API Keys, HMAC Signing and OAuth Client Credentials for Service-to-Service Auth
articles.scope: Expands the existing stub. Contrasts transport-layer identity (mTLS proves which service is calling) with possession of a bearer string, and adds HMAC request signing and client credentials as middle grounds. Covers issuing and rotating certificates through an internal CA or a service mesh, sidecar vs in-app TLS, and partner and broker APIs, so the reader can choose a method per integration and plan its rotation.

articles.title: Non-Human Identities and AI Agent Delegation
articles.scope: Inventories non-human identities (service accounts, keys, bots, workloads, agents), their governance gaps and stale credentials. Contrasts delegation with impersonation and covers token-exchange chains with act and may_act claims, transaction tokens and identity chaining drafts, the credential-broker (token vault) pattern, human approval through CIBA and RAR (RFC 9396), and attributable audit. MCP authorization belongs to ai/protocols, least agency and human-in-the-loop to security/ai-security, and Microsoft Entra Agent ID and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity to their provider pages.

articles.title: Decentralized Identity: W3C Verifiable Credentials, DIDs and OpenID4VC
articles.scope: Explains the issuer-holder-verifier triangle, W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0, DIDs, SD-JWT (RFC 9901) with SD-JWT VC (draft), ISO mDL, OpenID4VCI and OpenID4VP (both final 1.0), and wallet-based federation in SP 800-63C-4. Contrasts verifiable credentials with federated SSO on privacy, revocation and trust registries, linking Entra Verified ID for the SC-100 decentralized-identity objective.

articles.title: Threat Modeling Fundamentals: The Four Questions, DFDs and Trust Boundaries
articles.scope: Teaches Shostack's four questions and the Threat Modeling Manifesto, and contrasts asset-centric, attacker-centric and software-centric modeling. Covers DFD elements, trust boundaries, assumptions and the outputs a model must produce, so the reader can draw a Mermaid DFD of their own system with its trust boundaries marked.

articles.title: Threat Modeling Methods Compared: STRIDE, PASTA, LINDDUN, Attack Trees, DREAD, ATASM, OCTAVE, Trike and VAST
articles.scope: Compares methods by goal, effort, output and audience. Covers STRIDE per element and per interaction, PASTA's seven stages, LINDDUN GO, PRO and MAESTRO (distinct from CSA's agentic-AI MAESTRO, which security/ai-security covers), attack trees, DREAD and its criticisms, ATASM, OCTAVE, Trike and VAST. Explains when to combine them, for example STRIDE for engineering plus LINDDUN for personal data.

articles.title: How to Threat Model an ASP.NET Core API and Angular SPA Slice with STRIDE, and Keep It Current
articles.scope: Runs one STRIDE session on a small slice (sign-in plus one order-placement flow): scope, DFD, threat enumeration, mitigations mapped to controls, and security test cases. Shows how to keep the model as code with pytm or OWASP Threat Dragon, compared with the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, and when to revisit it. The full model of the reader's stack lives in practice/threat-models.

articles.title: Threat Modeling Cloud-Native and Multi-Cloud Systems: Management Plane, Identity, Tenancy and Shared Responsibility
articles.scope: Adds the provider management plane, IAM, CI/CD and managed services as DFD elements and trust boundaries. Works through the cloud-specific risks CCSP 4.3 lists (shared technology, CSP insiders, lack of visibility and control, jurisdiction) plus IAM misconfiguration and cross-tenant paths. The output is mapped to the controls in security/cloud-security.

articles.title: MITRE ATT&CK, D3FEND and CAPEC as Threat-Modeling Inputs, Contrasted with the Cyber Kill Chain and Diamond Model
articles.scope: Explains ATT&CK v20 (October 2026): tactics including Stealth and Defense Impairment, techniques, sub-techniques, detection strategies, and AI-related techniques mapped to MITRE ATLAS in security/ai-security. Contrasts it with D3FEND 1.0's defensive ontology, CAPEC attack patterns, the linear Cyber Kill Chain and the Diamond Model, which SY0-801 5.5 lists as reference sources and whose glossary terms belong to detection-response. Shows how to turn these into threat-model inputs and coverage maps.

articles.title: OWASP Top 10:2025 Explained with C# and Python
articles.scope: Covers A01 Broken Access Control to A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, with root causes, real examples, vulnerable and fixed snippets, and mapped CWEs. Explains the changes from 2021: SSRF folded into A01, Security Misconfiguration up to A02, A03 Software Supply Chain Failures widened, A07 renamed Authentication Failures, A09 renamed Security Logging and Alerting Failures, and A10 new. Each category links its deeper article.

articles.title: OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023): BOLA, BOPLA, BFLA and Friends
articles.scope: Covers API1 to API10 of the 2023 edition and disambiguates object-, property- and function-level authorization failures. Also covers resource consumption, sensitive business flows, SSRF, inventory and unsafe consumption of third-party APIs, with fixes in ASP.NET Core and FastAPI and links to gateway and WAF controls.

articles.title: OWASP Top 10 vs ASVS vs CWE Top 25: Awareness Lists, Verification Standards and Weakness Taxonomies
articles.scope: Explains why the Top 10 is an awareness document and not a standard, how ASVS 5.0.0 (17 chapters, levels 1-3, IDs v5.0.0-x.y.z) becomes testable requirements, and how CWE classifies root causes, contrasted with CVE and CVSS from detection-response. Afterwards the reader can build an ASVS-based requirements and test plan.

articles.title: Defining and Enforcing Secure Coding Standards in .NET and Python
articles.scope: Derives a team standard from ASVS and the CWE Top 25 and enforces it with .NET code-analysis security rules, custom Roslyn or Semgrep rules, and Bandit for Python. Adds review checklists, a documented exception process and adoption metrics.

articles.title: Injection Attacks: SQL, NoSQL, OS Command, LDAP and Template Injection
articles.scope: Shows injection as data interpreted as code across SQL (EF Core, Dapper, SQLAlchemy), NoSQL, OS command, LDAP, XPath, server-side template, header and log injection. Contrasts the defenses: parameterization, allow-list input validation, contextual output encoding and least-privilege database accounts. Links prompt injection in security/ai-security as the LLM-era analogue.

articles.title: XSS vs CSRF vs Clickjacking: Browser-Side Attacks and Defenses
articles.scope: Contrasts reflected, stored and DOM XSS with CSRF and clickjacking: who is tricked, which credentials are abused and which defenses apply. Covers Angular sanitization and its bypass APIs, CSP and Trusted Types, secure cookie attributes, anti-forgery tokens, frame-ancestors and HSTS, and explains why CORS relaxes the same-origin policy rather than stopping CSRF.

articles.title: SSRF, Path Traversal, Insecure Deserialization, XXE and Race Conditions
articles.scope: Covers SSRF (now part of A01:2025) against metadata endpoints and internal services; the IMDSv2 vs Azure IMDS contrast lives in cloud/compare. Also covers path traversal, upload abuse, XXE, TOCTOU races and egress controls. On deserialization, BinaryFormatter is treated as a legacy risk (removed in .NET 9 unless the unsupported compatibility package is added), and the current risks are Json.NET TypeNameHandling, any polymorphic or XML serializer configuration that lets the payload choose the type, and Python pickle and unsafe YAML.

articles.title: Secure Error and Exception Handling: Failing Closed, Problem Details and Leak-Free Errors
articles.scope: Addresses OWASP A10:2025 and SY0-801 unsafe exception handling. Authorization and crypto paths fail closed, clients get RFC 9457 problem details without stack traces, resources and transactions are cleaned up, and the user message is kept separate from the log record. Contrasts ASP.NET Core exception middleware and ProblemDetails with FastAPI exception handlers.

articles.title: Security Logging and Audit Trails for Applications: What to Log, Tamper Evidence and PII Hygiene
articles.scope: Addresses OWASP A09:2025 and CCSP 2.8. Covers which security events to log (authentication, authorization failures, admin actions, validation failures), structured logs with correlation IDs (Serilog, OpenTelemetry, Python logging), log-injection defenses, and tamper evidence through hash chains and WORM storage. Also covers attribution and chain of custody, and PII masking; SIEM belongs to detection-response.

articles.title: SAST vs DAST vs IAST vs SCA vs Fuzzing vs RASP
articles.scope: Compares techniques by when they run, what they see, their false-positive and false-negative profiles and their place in the pipeline. Adds black-, gray- and white-box (unknown, partially known, known environment) testing, abuse- and misuse-case testing, QA, coverage analysis, interface and API testing, and attack simulation. Examples use CodeQL, Semgrep and ZAP (formerly OWASP ZAP, now ZAP by Checkmarx); penetration testing links to detection-response and CI wiring to devops/ci-cd.

articles.title: WAF vs API Gateway vs RASP vs Database Activity Monitoring vs XML Firewall
articles.scope: Compares the CCSP 4.6 supplemental components by what each sees and blocks, where it sits, its false-positive behavior, known bypasses and latency, then combines them into layered designs. WAF product depth stays in network-security and the provider folders.

articles.title: Secure SDLC Frameworks and Maturity Models: NIST SSDF, OWASP SAMM, BSIMM, Microsoft SDL and CMM
articles.scope: Compares SSDF 1.1 (1.2 in draft), OWASP SAMM, BSIMM, Microsoft SDL, SAFECode guidance and CMM/CMMI. Places them against development methodologies (Agile, DevOps, DevSecOps, SAFe) and the Integrated Product Team, and covers SSDF attestation and SBOM requirements, shift left vs shift everywhere, and security champions. Afterwards the reader can assess a team and pick a framework.

articles.title: Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure, Bug Bounties and Security Advisories
articles.scope: Producer-side steps: publish a vulnerability disclosure policy and security.txt (RFC 9116), take in and triage reports per ISO/IEC 29147 and 30111, obtain CVE IDs through a CNA, and publish CSAF advisories with VEX. Contrasts bug bounties with VDPs and explains safe harbor; consumer-side vulnerability management belongs to detection-response.

articles.title: Secrets in Code: Detection, Push Protection, Rotation and Remediation
articles.scope: Explains how hardcoded secrets leak through repos, images, logs and CI variables, and contrasts pattern-based with entropy-based detection, pre-commit hooks and server-side push protection. Gives a remediation runbook built on the rule that rewriting history never helps without rotation, plus safe local development with .NET user-secrets and Python keyring or untracked .env files. Platform configuration for GH-500 belongs to devops/ci-cd.

articles.title: Memory Safety: Buffer Overflows, Use-After-Free and Memory-Safe Languages
articles.scope: Explains memory-corruption classes and the mitigations ASLR, DEP/NX, stack canaries, CFG and CET shadow stacks. Contrasts memory-safe managed runtimes (C#, including unsafe and Span) and Rust with C and C++, and shows where Python native extensions bring the risk back. CISA and NSA memory-safety guidance is background for the 'memory safe' languages item in CISSP 2027 8.2.

articles.title: Wasm Sandboxing vs Process, Container, gVisor and microVM Isolation
articles.scope: Expands the existing stub, correcting its claim that containers start with broad access: OCI containers get namespaces, dropped capabilities and a default seccomp profile, but share the host kernel's syscall surface. Compares processes, containers, gVisor, Firecracker microVMs and WebAssembly with WASI 0.3 deny-by-default capability imports on escape surface, cold start, density and fit for MCP tool runners and agent code execution. Kubernetes RuntimeClass configuration belongs to devops/kubernetes.

articles.title: Software Supply Chain Threats: From Dependency Confusion to Build Compromise
articles.scope: Classifies attacks on source, build, dependencies and distribution against SLSA's threat model: dependency confusion, typosquatting, starjacking, maintainer takeover, malicious updates, CI/CD poisoning and build compromise. Case studies are SolarWinds, xz-utils, the tj-actions/changed-files compromise (CVE-2025-30066) and the Shai-Hulud npm worm (2025). Maps these to OWASP A03:2025, CISSP SCRM and ISO/IEC 27036, and links the hardware supply-chain article.

articles.title: SBOMs: SPDX 3.0 vs CycloneDX 1.7, Generation and Consumption
articles.scope: Covers what an SBOM is for (inventory, licensing, vulnerability response) and its minimum elements. Compares SPDX 3.0.1 (ISO/IEC 5962:2021 standardizes 2.2.1) with CycloneDX 1.7 (ECMA-424 2nd edition) on data model, profiles, VEX support and tooling, and shows generation for .NET, Python and container images, plus CBOMs. AI BOMs belong to security/ai-security.

articles.title: VEX: Communicating Exploitability with CSAF, OpenVEX and CycloneDX
articles.scope: Explains why SBOM-driven scanning is noisy and how VEX statements (not_affected, affected, fixed, under_investigation, with justifications) cut the noise. Compares the CSAF 2.0 VEX profile, OpenVEX and CycloneDX VEX, and shows how to triage a CVE in a shipped product using EPSS and KEV context from detection-response.

articles.title: SLSA v1.2, Build Provenance and in-toto Attestations
articles.scope: Teaches the SLSA v1.2 Build track (L0-L3) and Source track (L1-L4) and what each level stops. Covers provenance predicates, in-toto statements and layouts, and reproducible and hermetic builds. Shows how to verify provenance at deploy or admission time with hosted-CI artifact attestations, as a commit-to-cluster flow linking devops/ci-cd and devops/kubernetes.

articles.title: Signing Artifacts: Sigstore Keyless vs Notary Project, GPG and Authenticode
articles.scope: Compares Sigstore keyless signing (cosign v3 bundles, short-lived Fulcio certificates bound to OIDC identities, the Rekor transparency log) with long-lived-key signing (Notary Project/Notation, OpenPGP/GPG, Authenticode, NuGet package signing). Covers trust roots, key compromise, offline verification, policy enforcement, code signing as a Security+ control, and the pitfall of checking the signature but not the signer identity.

articles.title: Dependency Hygiene for NuGet, npm and PyPI
articles.scope: Step-by-step hardening: lockfiles and pinning, NuGet package source mapping, npm scopes and provenance, and trusted publishing on PyPI, npm and nuget.org. Also covers npm's post-Shai-Hulud token and 2FA hardening, pip hash-checking mode, private feeds and upstream mirrors, Dependabot or Renovate, and OpenSSF Scorecard. Each step names the attack it blocks.

articles.title: Hardware and Firmware Supply Chain: Counterfeits, Implants, Silicon Root of Trust, PUFs, Secure and Measured Boot
articles.scope: Covers product tampering, counterfeits and implants (CISSP 1.11), hardware roots of trust including open designs such as Caliptra, PUFs, TPM-backed measured boot and remote attestation, UEFI secure boot, firmware signing and update integrity, and IoT/embedded devices. Contrasts secure boot (blocks) with measured boot (records), and explains how cloud providers attest their own hardware.

articles.title: Assessing Acquired Software: COTS vs Open Source vs Third-Party Components vs Managed Services and SaaS
articles.scope: For each category, compares the available evidence (SBOM, SCA results, attestations, pen-test reports, SOC 2), integrity and authenticity checks, licensing, update responsibility and exit risk, including validated open source. The contract and TPRM process belongs to security/grc.

articles.title: Cryptography Fundamentals: Symmetric vs Asymmetric, Modes, AEAD and Key Lengths
articles.scope: Contrasts symmetric with asymmetric encryption and block with stream ciphers. Covers ECB, CBC, CTR and GCM, why AEAD (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) is the default, IVs and nonces, key lengths and security strength, CSPRNGs, and how encoding and obfuscation differ from encryption. Uses the safe APIs in .NET System.Security.Cryptography and Python's cryptography package.

articles.title: Hashes vs MACs vs Digital Signatures vs Encryption
articles.scope: Separates integrity (hash), keyed authenticity (HMAC) and non-repudiation (RSA-PSS, ECDSA, Ed25519, ML-DSA) from confidentiality. Covers SHA-2 vs SHA-3, length extension, pure vs pre-hash signing, hash chains and Merkle trees, and why MACs cannot give non-repudiation. Afterwards the reader can pick the right primitive for a webhook, token, download or audit log.

articles.title: Password Hashing and Key Derivation: Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, PBKDF2 and HKDF
articles.scope: Explains why fast hashes are wrong for passwords and covers salt, pepper, key stretching and memory hardness. Compares Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt and PBKDF2 using the OWASP work factors, and contrasts them with HKDF for high-entropy input. Covers the ASP.NET Core Identity hasher, Python argon2-cffi, and upgrading hashes in place.

articles.title: TLS 1.3 Deep Dive: Handshake, Forward Secrecy, 0-RTT, ECH and Hybrid Post-Quantum Key Exchange
articles.scope: Walks through the TLS 1.3 handshake, ECDHE and forward secrecy, cipher suites, resumption and 0-RTT replay risk, and downgrade protection. Covers ECH (RFC 9849) and hybrid key exchange: RFC 9954 defines the design and RFC 10024 the ML-KEM groups (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024). Contrasts TLS 1.2 and load-balancer termination with end-to-end TLS, with Kestrel and Python ssl configuration.

articles.title: Secure Channels Compared: TLS vs SSH vs IPsec vs WireGuard vs End-to-End Messaging
articles.scope: Compares the protocols by layer, authentication model, key exchange and what each actually protects. Includes SSH keys vs SSH certificates, and the Signal protocol and MLS (RFC 9420) for end-to-end encrypted messaging. IPsec and VPN design depth stays in security/network-security.

articles.title: PKI and Certificate Lifecycle: Chains, Revocation, Transparency and 47-Day Certificates
articles.scope: Explains X.509, roots of trust, root and intermediate CAs, CSRs, DV/OV/EV, SAN and wildcard certificates, self-signed vs third-party certificates, key escrow, CT, CAA, private CAs, ACME, and why pinning usually backfires. Revocation is taught as it works today: SC-063 made CRLs mandatory and OCSP optional for public TLS, Let's Encrypt shut down OCSP in 2025, and browsers rely on CRLite and CRLSets, while OCSP remains exam vocabulary and is still used in private PKI. Ends with the SC-081 schedule (200 days from March 2026, 100 from March 2027, 47 from March 2029) that makes automation mandatory.

articles.title: Key Management, HSMs and Envelope Encryption
articles.scope: Covers the key lifecycle (SP 800-57), DEK/KEK hierarchies, envelope encryption, rotation vs re-encryption, crypto-shredding and escrow. Contrasts HSM, KMS, TPM and TEE, the FIPS 140-3 levels, and provider-managed vs CMK vs BYOK vs HYOK keys. The neutral pattern and the C# and Python code live here, with links to Key Vault, Managed HSM, AWS KMS and CloudHSM.

articles.title: Secrets Management: Vaults, Dynamic Secrets, Leasing, Secret Zero and Rotation
articles.scope: Separates secrets from keys and compares central stores (HashiCorp Vault, OpenBao, and provider stores, linked). Covers dynamic short-lived credentials and leases, solving secret zero with workload identity, injection through the Secrets Store CSI driver or External Secrets vs environment variables vs files, dual-secret rotation, and access auditing.

articles.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and Migration Planning
articles.scope: Explains the quantum threat (Shor, Grover, harvest now decrypt later), FIPS 203, 204 and 205, FN-DSA (FIPS 206, in development) and HQC as the backup KEM, and contrasts PQC with QKD. Covers hybrid PQ/T designs, the NIST IR 8547 draft timeline (deprecate after 2030, disallow after 2035) and CNSA 2.0. Ends with a crypto-agility and CBOM migration plan.

articles.title: Cryptographic Attacks and Misuse: Cryptanalysis, Side Channels and Implementation Pitfalls
articles.scope: Covers the CISSP 3.7 catalogue: brute force, ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext and chosen-ciphertext attacks, frequency analysis, implementation, side-channel, timing and fault-injection attacks, and adversary-in-the-middle. Adds birthday attacks, padding oracles, nonce reuse and protocol downgrade. Contrasts breaking the math with breaking the implementation, using real CVEs to show why you should use vetted libraries.

articles.title: Active Directory Hardening and the Enterprise Access Model: Tiering, Attacks, Defender for Identity and PAWs
articles.scope: Wave 4. Models: the legacy tier model vs the enterprise access model (control plane, management plane, data and workload plane, user and app access), privileged access workstations and intermediaries. Attacks: Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, DCSync, golden and silver tickets, pass-the-hash, AD CS ESC abuses, and dMSA abuse (BadSuccessor) on Windows Server 2025. Controls: Protected Users, gMSA, AES-only Kerberos, LAPS, krbtgt rotation, AD CS hardening, and treating Entra Connect and Cloud Sync servers as tier 0. Detection and resilience: Defender for Identity sensors and posture assessments, and AD forest recovery. It links to directory-services-ldap-kerberos, privileged-access-management-and-jit and identity-attacks-compared.

terms.definition: The access-control model of authentication (verify who a subject is), authorization (decide what it may do) and accounting (record what it did).
An authorization model that decides each request by evaluating policies over attributes of the subject, resource, action and environment, such as department, data classification or time.
A requirements artifact describing how a malicious or careless actor could misuse a feature, turned into security requirements and negative tests.
A list attached to an object naming which subjects may perform which operations on it; ACLs are the object columns of an access control matrix, and capability lists are its subject rows.
A small space with two interlocking doors, only one of which can open at a time, so a person is held and verified before entering a secure area, defeating tailgating.
A periodic or event-driven attestation in which owners or managers confirm or revoke each identity's group memberships, roles and application access.
A credential issued by an authorization server for a specific resource server (its audience) that represents the scopes and permissions granted to a client.
Restoring access after authenticators are lost or compromised, which must re-establish identity at least as strongly as normal sign-in or it becomes the weakest path.
The IETF protocol (RFC 8555), popularized by Let's Encrypt, that automates domain validation and certificate issuance and renewal.
A well-resourced, often state-linked actor that gains and keeps long-term, stealthy access to a target to pursue strategic goals such as espionage.
An attack in which an adversary sits between two parties to read, relay or alter traffic, such as a reverse-proxy phishing site that relays a user's sign-in and MFA to steal the session.
The NIST symmetric block cipher (FIPS 197) with a 128-bit block and 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys, normally used in an authenticated mode such as GCM.
A static secret string sent with requests to identify and authorize a calling application; it proves only possession of the string, so it must be stored, rotated and scoped carefully.
A permission granted to an application itself and used without a signed-in user through the client credentials grant, typically requiring admin consent because it applies across the tenant.
An attack that requests Kerberos AS-REP messages for accounts that do not require pre-authentication, then cracks the encrypted part offline to recover their passwords.

Cryptography with a mathematically linked key pair, where anyone can encrypt to or verify with the public key but only the private-key holder can decrypt or sign; it is used for key exchange and signatures, not bulk data.
A four-step threat modeling approach, popularized by Brook Schoenfield, that analyzes the architecture, enumerates threats and attack surfaces, then selects mitigations.
aliases: Architecture, Threats, Attack Surfaces and Mitigations

terms.definition: The total set of points where an unauthorized party could interact with a system, including interfaces, APIs, code paths, identities, dependencies and people.
A hierarchical diagram that breaks an attacker's goal into AND/OR sub-goals down to concrete steps, which can be annotated with cost, likelihood or required skill.

An encryption mode, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, that provides confidentiality and integrity together, rejecting tampered ciphertext and optionally authenticating unencrypted associated data.
The process of verifying that a subject (person, device, workload or agent) is who or what it claims to be, using one or more credentials.
The NIST SP 800-63-4 measure (AAL1 to AAL3) of confidence in an authentication event; syncable authenticators such as synced passkeys can reach AAL2 but not AAL3.
Assurance that data, a message or a party is genuine and comes from its claimed source; CISSP lists it alongside confidentiality, integrity, availability and non-repudiation.
The decision about whether an authenticated subject may perform a specific action on a specific resource, made by evaluating policy, roles, attributes or relationships.
The OAuth grant in which the user authenticates at the authorization server through a browser redirect and the client exchanges the returned short-lived code for tokens, protected by PKCE.
The OAuth component that authenticates the resource owner and client and issues access and refresh tokens; in OIDC it is also the OpenID provider.

The OpenID Foundation Authorization API 1.0 (final), which standardizes the subject-action-resource-context request a policy enforcement point sends to any policy decision point and the decision it gets back.

The browser-app architecture recommended by RFC 10017 (BCP 212) in which a server-side component acts as the confidential OAuth client, keeps tokens out of JavaScript and gives the SPA only an HttpOnly cookie.
A hardened, monitored intermediary host through which administrators reach protected networks or servers, so access control, session recording and audit happen in one place.
A token that grants access to whoever presents it, with no proof of key possession, so a stolen token works until it expires or is revoked.
A formal confidentiality model that enforces 'no read up' (simple security property) and 'no write down' (star property) between classification levels.
A formal integrity model whose simple integrity axiom ('no read down') and star integrity axiom ('no write up') stop lower-integrity subjects from corrupting higher-integrity data.
Finding hash collisions in roughly the square root of the output space (2^(n/2) work for an n-bit hash) because of the birthday paradox, which is why collision resistance needs long digests.
Testing with no knowledge of internal design or source, as an outside attacker would; gray-box (partially known environment) testing sits between it and white-box testing.
The construction that applies a block cipher to messages longer than one block (ECB, which is insecure, CBC, CTR or GCM), determining confidentiality, integrity and parallelism.
A highly protected, rarely used and heavily monitored account kept outside normal dependencies so administrators can regain control when standard sign-in or policy enforcement fails.
A model that prevents conflicts of interest by blocking a subject's access to one client's data once it has accessed a competitor's data in the same conflict class.
A model in which the customer generates key material, usually in its own HSM, and securely imports it into a cloud key service so it controls the key's origin and lifecycle.
An API flaw (API5:2023) in which callers can invoke administrative or other privileged operations because the server checks authentication but not the caller's right to that function.
An API flaw (API1:2023) in which the server does not check that the caller may access the specific object identified in the request, so changing an ID exposes other users' data.
An API flaw (API3:2023) that exposes or lets callers modify object properties they should not see or change, such as over-returned fields or a mass-assigned isAdmin flag.
Systematically trying every possible password or key until the right one is found, made infeasible by enough key length, slow hashing and lockout or rate limits.
A descriptive model, published annually, that reports which software security activities real organizations perform so others can benchmark against them.
Writing past the end of a fixed-size memory buffer, which can corrupt adjacent data or control flow and lead to code execution in memory-unsafe languages.
A program that pays external researchers for valid, in-scope vulnerability reports under published rules and safe-harbor terms.
Signed, verifiable metadata describing how an artifact was built: the builder, source revision, build instructions and input materials.
A DNS record (RFC 8659) listing which CAs may issue certificates for a domain; publicly trusted CAs must check it before issuance.
The OpenID SSF profile (1.0 final) defining events such as session revoked, credential change and device compliance change so receivers can re-evaluate access immediately.

An authorization model in which holding an unforgeable, attenuable reference or token naming specific resources and actions is the permission, which removes ambient authority and resists confused-deputy attacks.
A five-level process maturity model (initial, repeatable, defined, managed, optimizing) whose successor, CMMI, is used to assess software development organizations.
MITRE's catalog of common attack patterns against software, each linked to the CWE weaknesses it exploits, useful for enumerating threats during design.
aliases: Common Attack Pattern Enumeration and Classification

terms.definition: An inventory of a system's cryptographic assets (algorithms, keys, certificates, protocols and libraries), supported by CycloneDX and used to plan post-quantum migration.
An open-source authorization policy language created by AWS and accepted into the CNCF Sandbox in October 2025, designed for fast, formally analyzable permit and forbid policies.
An entity that verifies certificate requests and signs X.509 certificates binding public keys to identities (here CA never means Conditional Access).
Authentication in which a user or device proves possession of the private key for an X.509 certificate, often on a smart card or TPM; PIV and CAC smart cards count as phishing-resistant.
An access token bound to the thumbprint of the client's mTLS certificate (RFC 8705), so resource servers accept it only over a TLS connection authenticated with that certificate.
Hard-coding the expected certificate or public key for a host in a client, which blocks rogue CAs but breaks on routine rotation and is now discouraged for most apps.
A signed, periodically published list of serial numbers a CA has revoked before expiry; for publicly trusted TLS certificates, CRLs are mandatory and OCSP is optional.
A message signed with the requester's private key that carries the public key and requested identity for a CA to verify before issuing a certificate.
A system of public, append-only logs (RFC 6962) in which CAs record issued TLS certificates so domain owners and browsers can detect mis-issuance.

The three core security objectives: confidentiality (only authorized parties can read information), integrity (no unauthorized alteration) and availability (timely, reliable access for authorized users).
An OpenID Connect flow in which a client asks the provider to authenticate or get approval from a user on a separate device out of band, useful for call-center, payment and agent-action approvals.
Tooling that discovers the effective permissions of human and machine identities across cloud accounts and right-sizes them by comparing granted with used permissions.
Consensus-developed secure configuration recommendations from the Center for Internet Security for operating systems, cloud platforms and applications, published as Level 1 and Level 2 profiles.
An integrity model in which users change constrained data items only through certified, well-formed transformation procedures, enforcing separation of duties with user-program-data access triples.
Tricking a user into clicking something on a hidden or disguised framed page, prevented with the CSP frame-ancestors directive or X-Frame-Options.
The OAuth grant in which a confidential client with no user present authenticates as itself (with a secret, signed JWT assertion, mTLS or federated token) to obtain an access token.
The NSA algorithm suite for U.S. national security systems, which mandates ML-KEM-1024, ML-DSA-87, AES-256, SHA-384/512 and stateful hash-based signatures, with the transition to complete by 2035.
Applying a digital signature to executables, scripts or packages so consumers can verify the publisher's identity and that the code has not changed since signing.
An injection attack in which untrusted input reaches a shell or process call and runs operating-system commands, prevented by avoiding shells and passing argument arrays.
Ready-made software bought from a vendor, whose security must be judged from vendor evidence, testing and contracts because the source is usually unavailable.
The international framework (ISO/IEC 15408) for evaluating IT products against a protection profile or security target at assurance levels EAL1 to EAL7, with certificates recognized under the CCRA.
An alternative safeguard that meets the intent of a required control when the primary control is impractical, such as extra monitoring for a legacy system that cannot be patched.
An attack in which a privileged program or agent is tricked into misusing its own authority for a less-privileged caller, such as a tool server using its broad token on attacker-chosen resources.
An attack that tricks a user or admin into consenting to a malicious OAuth app, giving it persistent API access without stealing a password.
An HTTP response header that tells the browser which script, style, frame and connection sources a page may use, limiting XSS and clickjacking (CSP here is not a cloud service provider).

Re-evaluating active sessions and tokens in near real time when security events occur, such as account disablement or a password or location change, shared through SSF and CAEP rather than waiting for expiry.
A process in which a finder reports a vulnerability privately and the vendor fixes it before details are published on an agreed timeline (ISO/IEC 29147 and 30111).
A browser mechanism by which a server relaxes the same-origin policy for specific origins, methods and headers; it controls who can read responses and does not prevent CSRF.
A facility design approach that uses natural surveillance, natural access control, territorial reinforcement and maintenance to discourage crime before technical controls are needed.
A component that holds users' delegated OAuth tokens or API keys and injects scoped, short-lived credentials into agent or tool calls, so agents never see long-lived secrets.
Automatically replaying username and password pairs leaked from one breach against other sites, exploiting password reuse.
A secured store that holds privileged or shared credentials, checks them out to authorized users or tools, records their use and rotates them afterwards.
An attack that makes a victim's browser send an unwanted, state-changing request to a site where the victim is authenticated, abusing automatically attached cookies.

An injection attack in which attacker-controlled script runs in a victim's browser in the context of a trusted site, in stored, reflected or DOM-based form, enabling session theft or actions as the user.
The point at which a biometric system's false acceptance and false rejection rates are equal; a lower CER indicates a more accurate system.

The study and practice of breaking cryptographic schemes, classed by attacker knowledge (ciphertext-only, known-plaintext, chosen-plaintext and chosen-ciphertext attacks) and including frequency analysis.
The ability to inventory and replace cryptographic algorithms, key sizes and parameters across systems through configuration rather than code rewrites, as the post-quantum transition requires.
Making data unrecoverable by destroying every copy of the keys that encrypt it, the practical sanitization method for cloud and multi-tenant storage.
A one-way function that maps any input to a fixed-size digest and resists preimage, second-preimage and collision attacks, used for integrity checks and inside signatures and MACs.
The OASIS standard (CSAF 2.0) for machine-readable security advisories, whose VEX profile states product status for specific vulnerabilities.
A random generator whose output stays unpredictable even to an attacker who sees earlier outputs, such as .NET RandomNumberGenerator or Python's secrets module, unlike System.Random or random.
The FIDO Alliance protocol that a browser or operating system uses to talk to an external authenticator over USB, NFC or Bluetooth to create and use FIDO2 credentials.
A key the customer creates and controls in the provider's key service (policy, rotation, disablement) while the provider performs the cryptographic operations; Azure and AWS both use the term.
MITRE's taxonomy of software and hardware weakness types (root causes such as CWE-89 SQL injection), from which the annual CWE Top 25 is derived.
The OWASP-originated bill-of-materials standard, currently 1.7 and standardized as ECMA-424 2nd edition, covering software, SaaS, hardware, cryptographic and ML BOMs as well as VEX.
Black-box testing of a running application by sending crafted requests and observing responses to find exploitable vulnerabilities, without access to source code.
The symmetric key that actually encrypts data, generated per object or dataset and stored only in wrapped form next to it.
A diagram of external entities, processes, data stores and data flows, annotated with trust boundaries, used as the system model for threat enumeration.
An attack in which an account with directory replication rights impersonates a domain controller to pull password hashes, including krbtgt's, through the replication protocol.
A W3C identifier (DID 1.0) whose controller proves control through keys listed in a resolvable DID document, without a central registry.
A strategy of layering independent, diverse controls so that bypassing or breaking any one layer does not by itself expose the protected asset.
An OAuth permission (scope) that lets an app act on behalf of a signed-in user, limited to the intersection of what the app was granted and what the user can do.
An attack in which a malicious public package reuses the name of an internal private package so that misconfigured package managers resolve the attacker's higher-versioned public copy.
The OAuth grant (RFC 8628) for input-constrained devices and CLIs, in which the device shows a user code that the user approves on a second device while the device polls for tokens.
A unique, verifiable identity for a device, typically a certificate or key protected by a TPM, established when the device is registered with or joined to a directory.
The current security state of a device, such as patch level, encryption, EDR status and configuration compliance, evaluated as a signal in access decisions.
A culture and practice that makes security a shared, automated part of DevOps pipelines and operations instead of a separate gate.
A key-agreement method in which two parties derive a shared secret over a public channel; ephemeral variants (DHE, ECDHE) provide forward secrecy in TLS.

A value computed with a private key over a message (often via its hash; Ed25519 and ML-DSA sign the message directly) that anyone with the public key can verify, giving integrity, authenticity and non-repudiation.
Replicating identities, groups and optionally password hashes from one directory to another, such as on-premises AD to a cloud directory, so users have one identity in both.
An access control model in which a resource's owner decides who may access it, typically through ACLs (not Windows Dynamic Access Control, also abbreviated DAC).
Forcing parties to negotiate an older protocol version or weaker cipher than both support so that a known weakness can be exploited, countered by TLS 1.3 downgrade protection and HSTS.
An OAuth mechanism (RFC 9449) that binds tokens to a client-held key by having the client sign a proof JWT for each request, so stolen tokens are useless without the private key.
A threat-rating mnemonic (damage, reproducibility, exploitability, affected users, discoverability) criticized for subjective, inconsistent scores; Microsoft no longer recommends it.
Public-key cryptography over elliptic-curve groups (ECDH, ECDSA, Ed25519) that matches RSA's security with much smaller keys and is equally vulnerable to quantum attack.
A TLS 1.3 extension (RFC 9849) that encrypts the ClientHello, including the server name, with a key published in DNS, hiding the destination from on-path observers.
Encryption in which only the communicating endpoints hold the keys, so servers and intermediaries relaying the data cannot read it, as in the Signal protocol or MLS.

Microsoft's successor to the AD tier model. It separates the control plane, the management plane, the data and workload plane, and user and app access, with privileged access pathways and intermediaries between them.
A specific access right, such as a group membership, role, license or application permission, that is granted, reviewed and revoked as a governed unit.

Encrypting data with a data encryption key and then encrypting that key with a key encryption key held in a KMS or HSM, so bulk data is encrypted locally and only small keys cross the key-service boundary.
Code, input or a technique that takes advantage of a specific vulnerability to cause unintended behavior such as code execution, data access or privilege gain.
A failure mode in which a control that fails stops enforcing and lets traffic or access through, favoring availability over security.
A failure mode designed to protect people and prevent harm, such as unlocking exit doors during a fire, which can conflict with keeping assets secure.
A failure mode in which a component that fails defaults to denying access or halting rather than continuing in a permissive state.
The proportion of impostor biometric attempts that are wrongly accepted (a Type II error), the error that matters most for security.
The proportion of legitimate users' biometric attempts that are wrongly rejected (a Type I error), the error that drives usability complaints.

The OpenID Foundation's high-assurance OAuth profile (Security Profile final February 2025), which requires PAR, PKCE, sender-constrained tokens via mTLS or DPoP, and private_key_jwt or mTLS client authentication.
A trust relationship across security domains in which a relying party accepts authentication assertions from an external identity provider instead of managing its own credentials for those users.
The NIST SP 800-63-4 measure (FAL1 to FAL3) of the strength of a federated assertion: how it is protected, presented and bound to the subscriber.
The FIDO Alliance and W3C standard set, made up of WebAuthn and CTAP, for origin-bound public-key authentication without shared secrets.
Encrypting individual fields or columns in the application or client before storage, so database administrators and compromised database hosts see only ciphertext.

The U.S. federal standard for cryptographic modules, aligned with ISO/IEC 19790, with four security levels validated through the joint NIST and Canadian CCCS CMVP; FIPS 140-2 validations became historical in September 2026.
The compact lattice-based signature scheme being standardized as FIPS 206 (still in development), offering smaller signatures than ML-DSA at the cost of harder implementation.
Encrypting an entire storage device, as BitLocker or LUKS do, which protects data on lost or stolen hardware but not from anyone using the running system.
Automatically feeding large volumes of malformed, random or mutated input to a program, often guided by code coverage, and watching for crashes, hangs or assertion failures.
Forging SAML assertions with a stolen identity-provider token-signing key, letting an attacker sign in to any federated service as any user without passing MFA.
A forged Kerberos ticket-granting ticket signed with a stolen KRBTGT key, giving an attacker arbitrary, long-lived domain access until that key is rotated twice.
A password, key or token written directly into source code, configuration or images, where version control, builds and logs copy it everywhere.
An immutable hardware component, such as boot ROM with fused keys, that starts the chain of trust by verifying the first firmware stage before any mutable code runs.
A tamper-resistant, typically FIPS 140-3 validated device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys so private key material never leaves it in plaintext.
A physical authenticator, such as a FIDO2 security key, smart card or OTP key fob, whose secret stays on dedicated hardware the user must possess.
Recording encrypted traffic or data today in order to decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists, which makes key exchange the first post-quantum migration priority.
A message authentication code (RFC 2104) built from a hash function and a secret key, immune to length extension and used for webhook signatures and JWT HS256.
A model in which keys stay in a customer-operated key service outside the cloud provider, so the provider can never decrypt the protected data, at a cost in availability and features.
Encryption that allows computation on ciphertexts so the decrypted result equals the same computation on plaintexts; fully homomorphic schemes remain orders of magnitude slower.

A code-based key-encapsulation mechanism that NIST selected in March 2025 as a backup to ML-KEM, built on different mathematics in case lattice schemes are broken; its standard is still being drafted.
A response header that tells browsers to use only HTTPS for a domain for a set period, defeating SSL-stripping downgrades; preload lists apply it before the first visit.
Combining a classical and a post-quantum key exchange so a session stays secure if either holds, as specified for TLS 1.3 in RFC 9954 with ML-KEM groups such as X25519MLKEM768 in RFC 10024.
Testing that instruments a running application from inside, usually through an agent, to observe tainted data flows while functional or DAST tests exercise it.
An OpenID Connect JWT, intended for the client and not for APIs, that asserts who authenticated, when, how and for which client.
The step in which a subject claims an identity, by presenting a username, account ID or certificate subject, before that claim is authenticated.
The NIST SP 800-63-4 measure (IAL1 to IAL3) of how rigorously an applicant's identity was proven at enrollment.
The discipline and tooling for managing identity lifecycles, entitlements, access requests, certifications and segregation-of-duties policies across systems.

Collecting and validating evidence such as documents, records or biometrics to confirm that an applicant is the real person they claim to be before issuing an account or credential (NIST SP 800-63A-4).
The system that authenticates subjects and issues the assertions or tokens about them that relying parties trust.
Acting fully as another identity, so downstream systems cannot tell the actor from the subject; delegation, by contrast, records both.
A deprecated OAuth grant that returned access tokens directly in the browser redirect URL, exposing them to leakage; the code grant with PKCE replaces it.
A CNCF Graduated framework and attestation format for recording, signing and verifying each step of a software supply chain, used as the envelope for SLSA provenance.
The level of risk before any controls or mitigations are applied, used as the baseline for judging how much the controls reduce it.
A per-message input to an encryption mode that makes identical plaintexts encrypt differently; CBC needs unpredictable IVs, while CTR and GCM need unique nonces.
Checking at a trust boundary, preferably with allow-lists, that input matches the expected type, length, format and range before processing it.

Deserializing untrusted data with a format or setting that lets the payload choose which types to instantiate, as with legacy .NET BinaryFormatter, Json.NET TypeNameHandling or Python pickle, which can lead to remote code execution.
Risk posed by people with legitimate access, such as employees, contractors or partners, who misuse it maliciously or cause harm accidentally.
Security capabilities that detect and respond to attacks on identity systems and credentials, such as token theft, directory attacks and risky sign-ins, rather than on endpoints or networks.
Periodically moving people between duties so that fraud or errors that depend on one person's continuous control are more likely to be discovered.
The identity lifecycle process that grants access when someone joins, adjusts it when they change roles and removes it promptly when they leave.
Granting a privilege only when it is requested and justified, for a limited time window, instead of holding it as a standing assignment.
Creating a user's account in an application at first sign-in from attributes in the federation assertion, instead of in advance; it never deprovisions on its own.
The JOSE format (RFC 7516) that encrypts a payload so only holders of the intended key can read it, adding confidentiality to integrity.
A JSON representation of a cryptographic key (RFC 7517); a JWK Set published at an issuer's jwks_uri lets relying parties fetch and rotate token-signing keys.
The JOSE format (RFC 7515) that protects a payload's integrity and authenticity with a digital signature or MAC while leaving the content readable.
A compact, URL-safe claims format (RFC 7519), usually signed as a JWS and sometimes encrypted as a JWE, used for ID tokens, access tokens and assertions.
Requesting Kerberos service tickets for accounts with service principal names and cracking them offline, since they are encrypted with keys derived from the service account's password.

A ticket-based authentication protocol in which a key distribution center issues a ticket-granting ticket and then service tickets, so clients never send passwords to services; it underpins Active Directory.
The principle that a system should stay secure even if everything about it except the key is public, so security rests on secrets that can be changed.
A function that derives cryptographic keys from a secret; HKDF expands high-entropy input such as a Diffie-Hellman shared secret, while password-based KDFs stretch low-entropy passwords.
A key, usually held in a KMS or HSM, used only to encrypt (wrap) other keys such as DEKs, so rotating it does not require re-encrypting bulk data.
Depositing copies of keys with a trusted third party or recovery agent so encrypted data can be recovered, or lawfully accessed, if the primary key holder is unavailable.

A service that centrally creates, stores, rotates, access-controls and audits cryptographic keys, often backed by HSMs and exposing encrypt, decrypt and sign APIs (a generic term; AWS KMS is one product).
Replacing a cryptographic key with a new version on a schedule or after suspected compromise, so new data uses the new key while retained old versions can still decrypt or verify existing data.
Making each guess of a low-entropy secret expensive by iterating or memory-hardening the derivation, as PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt and Argon2id do.
Signing with an ephemeral key whose certificate is issued for minutes to a verified OIDC identity and recorded in a transparency log, so there is no long-lived private key to protect.
A protocol for querying and modifying hierarchical directory services, also used for simple-bind authentication, which must be protected with LDAPS or StartTLS.
The principle that every user, service, workload or agent holds only the permissions its specific task requires, for only as long as it needs them.
Appending data to a message and computing a valid hash for it from only the original hash and length, possible with Merkle-Damgård hashes such as SHA-256 when used as hash(key || message).

A privacy threat modeling framework covering linking, identifying, non-repudiation, detecting, data disclosure, unawareness and unintervenability, and non-compliance, offered in GO, PRO and MAESTRO variants.
A generated file, such as packages.lock.json, package-lock.json or uv.lock, that pins every direct and transitive dependency to exact versions, often with hashes, for reproducible installs.
A legitimate-looking software or package update that delivers attacker code through the trusted update channel, as in SolarWinds or a hijacked maintainer account.
An access control model in which a central authority enforces access based on security labels and clearances that users cannot change, as in SELinux or classified systems.
A boot process that records a hash of each loaded component into TPM registers without blocking anything, so a verifier can later attest what actually ran.
The property of a language or runtime that prevents out-of-bounds access, use-after-free and similar memory corruption, which underlie buffer overflows and many critical CVEs.

A short tag computed from a message and a shared secret key that proves integrity and authenticity to key holders but cannot provide non-repudiation (not mandatory access control or a media access control address).
An attack that floods a user with MFA push requests until they approve one, countered by number matching, rate limits and phishing-resistant methods.
A minimal virtual machine, such as a Firecracker microVM, that gives each workload its own guest kernel behind hardware virtualization while starting in milliseconds.
MITRE's knowledge base of real-world adversary tactics, techniques and sub-techniques, with groups, software, mitigations and detection strategies; v20 (October 2026) is current.
aliases: Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge

terms.definition: MITRE's knowledge graph of defensive techniques (1.0 released January 2025) that maps countermeasures to the digital artifacts they act on and the ATT&CK techniques they counter.
The lattice-based digital signature algorithm standardized in FIPS 204 (August 2024) as the primary post-quantum replacement for RSA and ECDSA signatures.
The lattice-based key-encapsulation mechanism standardized in FIPS 203 (August 2024) for establishing shared secrets, deployed in TLS 1.3 inside hybrid groups such as X25519MLKEM768.
TLS in which both client and server present and validate X.509 certificates, so the calling service is authenticated at the transport layer as well as the server.
Authentication that requires at least two different factor types, chosen from something you know, something you have and something you are.
The principle that a subject may access specific information only when a legitimate task requires it, even when its clearance or role would otherwise allow access.
NIST SP 800-218, a set of outcome-based secure development practices grouped as prepare, protect, produce and respond; version 1.1 is final and 1.2 is a draft.

Any identity used by software rather than a person, such as service accounts, API keys, workload identities, bots and AI agents, which typically outnumber human identities and lack lifecycle governance.
Assurance that the originator of an action or message cannot credibly deny it, typically provided by a digital signature from a key bound to a unique identity plus trustworthy logs.
A value that must never repeat for a given key or context, as in AES-GCM, OIDC authentication requests or replay protection; reusing one can be catastrophic.
